claim: Munc13s are essential for synaptic vesicle (SV) docking and priming.
source: Munc13s are essential for SV docking and priming, and we systematically analyzed their role in LDCV exocytosis using chromaffin cells lacking individual isoforms.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature in the manuscript.

claim: Munc13-2 plays a fundamental role in LDCV exocytosis.
source: We show that particularly Munc13-2 plays a fundamental role in LDCV exocytosis, but in contrast to synapses lacking Munc13s, the corresponding chromaffin cells do not exhibit a vesicle docking defect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing reduced LDCV release in Munc13-2 knockout cells.

claim: Chromaffin cells lacking Munc13s do not exhibit a vesicle docking defect.
source: We show that particularly Munc13-2 plays a fundamental role in LDCV exocytosis, but in contrast to synapses lacking Munc13s, the corresponding chromaffin cells do not exhibit a vesicle docking defect.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing normal LDCV docking in Munc13-deficient chromaffin cells.

claim: ubMunc13-2 and Munc13-1 confer Ca2+-dependent LDCV priming with similar affinities but distinct kinetics.
source: We further demonstrate that ubMunc13-2 and Munc13-1 confer Ca2+-dependent LDCV priming with similar affinities, but distinct kinetics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and mathematical modeling showing similar Ca2+ affinities but different kinetic properties.

claim: There is an early LDCV priming step that is strongly dependent upon Munc13s.
source: Using a mathematical model, we identify an early LDCV priming step that is strongly dependent upon Munc13s.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling of experimental data.

claim: The molecular steps of SV and LDCV priming are very similar.
source: Our data demonstrate that the molecular steps of SV and LDCV priming are very similar while SV and LDCV docking mechanisms are distinct.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental results with known SV mechanisms.

claim: SV and LDCV docking mechanisms are distinct.
source: Our data demonstrate that the molecular steps of SV and LDCV priming are very similar while SV and LDCV docking mechanisms are distinct.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that LDCVs dock normally without Munc13s while SVs do not.

claim: Munc13s mediate the formation of SNARE complexes at vesicular release sites.
source: At the molecular level, this morphological phenotype most likely corresponds to a role of Munc13s in mediating the formation of SNARE complexes at vesicular release sites (Hammarlund et al., 2007; Hammarlund et al., 2008; Imig et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2011; 2013; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Munc13 family consists of five members: Munc13-1 (Unc13a), Munc13-2 (Unc13b), Munc13-3 (Unc13c), Baiap3, and Munc13-4 (Unc13d).
source: The Munc13 family consists of five members, Munc13-1 (Unc13a), Munc13-2 (Unc13b), Munc13-3 (Unc13c), the brain specific angiogenesis inhibitor I-associated protein 3 (Baiap3), and the non-neuronal isoform Munc13-4 (Unc13d) (Koch et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Genetic deletion of Unc13a and Unc13b completely eliminates SV exocytosis in hippocampal neurons.
source: Genetic deletion of Unc13a and Unc13b completely eliminates SV exocytosis in hippocampal neurons (Varoqueaux et al., 2002), and selectively reduces synaptic vs. extrasynaptic exocytosis of neuronal LDCVs (van de Bospoort et al., 2012), which indicates that SV and LDCV exocytosis at active zones is mediated by similar molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of Unc13a and Unc13b selectively reduces synaptic vs. extrasynaptic exocytosis of neuronal LDCVs.
source: Genetic deletion of Unc13a and Unc13b completely eliminates SV exocytosis in hippocampal neurons (Varoqueaux et al., 2002), and selectively reduces synaptic vs. extrasynaptic exocytosis of neuronal LDCVs (van de Bospoort et al., 2012), which indicates that SV and LDCV exocytosis at active zones is mediated by similar molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In C. elegans and Drosophila, Unc-13/dUnc-13 selectively regulate SV release, whereas CAPS/Unc-31 specifically regulate LDCV release.
source: By contrast, studies in C. elegans and Drosophila have shown that Unc-13/dUnc-13 selectively regulate SV release, whereas the Ca2+-dependent activator proteins for secretion (CAPS/Unc-31) specifically regulate LDCV release (Hammarlund et al., 2008; Renden et al., 2001; Speese et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In mammals, Munc13s and CAPSs perform non-redundant functions critical for both SV and LDCV exocytosis in neurons.
source: In mammals, Munc13s and CAPSs appear to perform non-redundant functions critical for both SV and LDCV exocytosis in neurons (Jockusch et al., 2007; van de Bospoort et al., 2012), as well as for LDCV exocytosis in neuroendocrine cells (Elhamdani et al., 1999; Kabachinski et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2006; Kwan et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2008; Speidel et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CAPS-1 and CAPS-2 are required for LDCV exocytosis in mammalian chromaffin cells.
source: Yet, to date, while CAPS-1 and CAPS-2 have been shown to be required for LDCV exocytosis in mammalian chromaffin cells (Liu et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2008), evidence that endogenous Munc13s are required for LDCV exocytosis is lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Evidence that endogenous Munc13s are required for LDCV exocytosis in mammalian chromaffin cells is lacking.
source: Yet, to date, while CAPS-1 and CAPS-2 have been shown to be required for LDCV exocytosis in mammalian chromaffin cells (Liu et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2008), evidence that endogenous Munc13s are required for LDCV exocytosis is lacking.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior studies examining endogenous Munc13s in chromaffin cells.

claim: Munc13-1 is barely detectable in perinatal adrenal gland.
source: Munc13-1 (*) is barely detectable in perinatal adrenal gland.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ubMunc13-2, but not bMunc13-2, is expressed in perinatal adrenal gland.
source: ubMunc13-2, but not bMunc13-2, is expressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Munc13-3 was not detected in perinatal adrenal gland.
source: Munc13-3 was not detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Baiap3 was detected in perinatal adrenal gland.
source: Baiap3 was detected, but not (E) Munc13-4.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Munc13-4 was not detected in perinatal adrenal gland.
source: Baiap3 was detected, but not (E) Munc13-4.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Munc13-1 and Baiap3 are mainly located in the adrenal medulla.
source: Munc13-1 and Baiap3 are mainly located in the medulla (Med), but ubMunc13-2 is present in cortex (Cort) as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data from dissected adrenal tissue shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ubMunc13-2 is present in both adrenal cortex and medulla.
source: Munc13-1 and Baiap3 are mainly located in the medulla (Med), but ubMunc13-2 is present in cortex (Cort) as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data from dissected adrenal tissue shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ubMunc13-2-EYFP is the only Munc13 isoform readily detectable in the adrenal gland using an antibody to GFP-derived tags.
source: We found that ubMunc13-2-EYFP is the only isoform readily detectable in the adrenal gland using an antibody to the GFP-derived tags (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data from knock-in mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deletion of Munc13-1 (Unc13a) did not markedly alter LDCV exocytosis compared to WT littermate controls.
source: Deletion of Munc13-1 (Unc13a), the major Munc13 isoform in SV exocytosis (Augustin et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002), did not markedly alter LDCV exocytosis compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 2A,D), nor did it affect the kinetics of the exocytotic burst (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2A,D.

claim: Deletion of Munc13-1 did not affect the kinetics of the exocytotic burst.
source: Deletion of Munc13-1 (Unc13a), the major Munc13 isoform in SV exocytosis (Augustin et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002), did not markedly alter LDCV exocytosis compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 2A,D), nor did it affect the kinetics of the exocytotic burst (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LDCV exocytosis in Unc13cKO chromaffin cells was not perturbed.
source: However, as expected, LDCV exocytosis in Unc13cKO chromaffin cells was not perturbed (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2B,D.

claim: LDCV exocytosis in Baiap3KO cells was intact.
source: Surprisingly, LDCV exocytosis in Baiap3KO cells was intact (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Baiap3KO cells did not show a release deficit when stimulated using a series of depolarization steps.
source: Furthermore, Baiap3KO cells also did not show a release deficit when we stimulated the cells using a series of depolarization steps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), nor did overexpression of Baiap3 in WT cells affect LDCV exocytosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by depolarization experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Overexpression of Baiap3 in WT cells did not affect LDCV exocytosis.
source: Furthermore, Baiap3KO cells also did not show a release deficit when we stimulated the cells using a series of depolarization steps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), nor did overexpression of Baiap3 in WT cells affect LDCV exocytosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Abrogation of ubMunc13-2 expression alone, irrespective of the Unc13a genotype, drastically diminished LDCV release.
source: By contrast, abrogation of ubMunc13-2 expression alone, irrespective of the Unc13a genotype, drastically diminished release (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: In the context of the Unc13bKO background, cells with Unc13aWT, Unc13aHet, and Unc13aKO genotypes showed a progressive reduction of LDCV release that depended on the number of Unc13a alleles present.
source: Furthermore, in the context of the Unc13bKO background, cells with Unc13aWT, Unc13aHet, and Unc13aKO genotypes showed a progressive reduction of LDCV release that depended on the number of Unc13a alleles present (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The fast burst component was reduced to 39%, 32%, and 27% of control levels in Unc13aWTUnc13bKO, Unc13aHetUnc13bKO, and Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells, respectively.
source: The fast and slow burst components were reduced to 39%, 32%, and 27%, and to 54%, 52%, and 42% of control levels, respectively (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The slow burst component was reduced to 54%, 52%, and 42% of control levels in Unc13aWTUnc13bKO, Unc13aHetUnc13bKO, and Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells, respectively.
source: The fast and slow burst components were reduced to 39%, 32%, and 27%, and to 54%, 52%, and 42% of control levels, respectively (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The rate of sustained release was reduced to 26%, 19%, and 12% of control levels in Unc13aWTUnc13bKO, Unc13aHetUnc13bKO, and Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells, respectively.
source: The rate of sustained release was reduced even more dramatically, to 26%, 19%, and 12% of control levels (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of capacitance measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The deletion of both Unc13a and Unc13b significantly delayed the onset of vesicular exocytosis triggered by flash photolysis.
source: The deletion of both Unc13a and Unc13b significantly delayed the onset of vesicular exocytosis triggered by flash photolysis, compared to control and Unc13aKOUnc13bHet cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of exocytosis delay shown in Figure 2H.

claim: ubMunc13-2 is the most critical isoform for LDCV release in chromaffin cells.
source: Thus, ubMunc13-2, the only isoform expressed from the Unc13b gene in mouse chromaffin cells, is the most critical isoform for LDCV release in this cell type.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that deletion of ubMunc13-2 has the most dramatic effect on LDCV release.

claim: In the absence of ubMunc13-2, endogenous Munc13-1 also regulates LDCV release.
source: Moreover, in its absence it becomes apparent that endogenous Munc13-1 also regulates LDCV release in this cell type.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that deletion of Munc13-1 in the Unc13bKO background further reduces LDCV release.

claim: The size of the RRP in Unc13bKO cells was reduced to 53% of WT levels in depolarization experiments.
source: We found a significant reduction in LDCV release; the size of the RRP in Unc13bKO cells was reduced to 53% of WT levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by depolarization experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Impaired release in Unc13bKO cells was already evident in response to the first 10-ms depolarization.
source: Strikingly, in the depolarization experiment, impaired release in Unc13bKO cells was already evident in response to the first 10-ms depolarization (Figure 3B), which implies that lack of ubMunc13-2 would even affect resting level catecholamine release driven by low frequency stimulation (Zhou and Misler, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by depolarization experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lack of ubMunc13-2 would affect resting level catecholamine release driven by low frequency stimulation.
source: Strikingly, in the depolarization experiment, impaired release in Unc13bKO cells was already evident in response to the first 10-ms depolarization (Figure 3B), which implies that lack of ubMunc13-2 would even affect resting level catecholamine release driven by low frequency stimulation (Zhou and Misler, 1995).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that release is impaired even with the first brief depolarization.

claim: Unc13bKO cells showed a dramatic reduction in spike frequency in amperometry experiments.
source: Unc13bKO cells showed a dramatic reduction in spike frequency (Figure 4B,C), whereas basic spike parameters such as duration, half-width, maximum amplitude, charge, rise time, and decay time were unchanged (Figure 4D–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by amperometry data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Basic spike parameters such as duration, half-width, maximum amplitude, charge, rise time, and decay time were unchanged in Unc13bKO cells.
source: Unc13bKO cells showed a dramatic reduction in spike frequency (Figure 4B,C), whereas basic spike parameters such as duration, half-width, maximum amplitude, charge, rise time, and decay time were unchanged (Figure 4D–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by amperometry data shown in Figure 4D–I.

claim: Amplitude, duration and charge of the spike foot signal were unchanged in Unc13bKO cells.
source: Amplitude, duration and charge of the spike foot signal, which is thought to reflect release during the initial formation of the fusion pore prior to full fusion, were also unchanged (Figure 4J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by amperometry data shown in Figure 4J–L.

claim: The number of spikes that showed foot signals was slightly reduced in Unc13bKO cells.
source: However, we found that the number of spikes that did show these foot signals was slightly reduced in Unc13bKO cells (Figure 4M), which may indicate that fusion pore dynamics are altered for some release events.
evidence: This claim is supported by amperometry data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: Fusion pore dynamics may be altered for some release events in Unc13bKO cells.
source: However, we found that the number of spikes that did show these foot signals was slightly reduced in Unc13bKO cells (Figure 4M), which may indicate that fusion pore dynamics are altered for some release events.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that fewer spikes show foot signals.

claim: LDCVs undergoing fusion in the absence of ubMunc13-2 do so without major alterations in fusion kinetics or vesicle content.
source: However, overall, the LDCVs undergoing fusion in the absence of ubMunc13-2 do so without major alterations in fusion kinetics or vesicle content.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that spike parameters are largely unchanged in Unc13bKO cells.

claim: Munc13-1 and ubMunc13-2 were both able to rescue the LDCV release deficit of Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells.
source: Interestingly, Munc13-1 and ubMunc13-2 were both able to rescue the LDCV release deficit of Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Rescue with ubMunc13-2 resulted in an enormous enhancement of LDCV exocytosis to levels that by far exceeded the amount of exocytosis typical of WT cells.
source: However, rescue with ubMunc13-2 resulted in an enormous enhancement of LDCV exocytosis to levels that by far exceeded the amount of exocytosis typical of WT cells, for both the exocytotic burst and the rate of sustained release (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The stronger enhancement of burst size and rate of sustained release in ubMunc13-2 expressing cells was not due to higher expression levels of ubMunc13-2.
source: The direct comparison of Munc13-1 and ubMunc13-2 expressing cells with matching EGFP fluorescence intensity confirmed that the stronger enhancement of burst size and rate of sustained release in ubMunc13-2 expressing cells was not due to higher expression levels of ubMunc13-2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of cells with matched fluorescence intensity shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of Baiap3 failed to rescue the LDCV release deficit of the Unc13aKOUnc13bKO chromaffin cells.
source: Overexpression of Baiap3 failed to rescue the LDCV release deficit of the Unc13aKOUnc13bKO chromaffin cells (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Munc13-4 was able to rescue LDCV exocytosis in Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells, albeit less efficiently than Munc13-1 or ubMunc13-2.
source: Yet, its closest relative, Munc13-4, which regulates SNARE-mediated vesicular exocytosis in the hematopoietic system (Feldmann et al., 2003; Shirakawa et al., 2004), was able to rescue LDCV exocytosis in Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells, albeit less efficiently than Munc13-1 or ubMunc13-2 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Individual Munc13 isoforms show inherent differences in their ability to promote LDCV release in chromaffin cells.
source: Thus, individual Munc13 isoforms appear to show inherent differences in their ability to promote LDCV release in chromaffin cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that different isoforms rescue LDCV release to different extents.

claim: Unc13aKOUnc13bKO chromaffin cells do not show an LDCV docking defect.
source: Quantitative analysis of 2D-EM images of Unc13aHetUnc13bHet (Figure 6A) and Unc13aKOUnc13bKO chromaffin cells (Figure 6B) did not reveal any differences in LDCV distribution within 2 μm of the plasma membrane (PM) (Figure 6C), in the number of membrane-proximal LDCVs within 40 nm of the PM (Figure 6D), or in the total number of LDCVs (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by 2D-EM analysis shown in Figure 6A–E.

claim: LDCV recruitment to the plasma membrane is intact in Munc13-deficient chromaffin cells.
source: From all LDCVs analyzed within 100 nm of the PM, the percentage of membrane-proximal LDCVs (0–40 nm) (Figure 6M) and their distribution (Figure 6L) was unaltered between both groups, indicating that LDCV recruitment to the PM is intact in Munc13-deficient chromaffin cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D-ET analysis shown in Figure 6L,M.

claim: The number of docked LDCVs was unchanged in Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells.
source: The number of docked LDCVs, defined as LDCVs in physical contact with the PM and assigned to the 0–4 nm bin in Figure 6L, and the number of docked LDCVs normalized to the number of membrane-proximal LDCVs (Figure 6N) were unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D-ET analysis shown in Figure 6L,N.

claim: Chromaffin cells can generate a full-sized pool of morphologically docked LDCVs in the absence of Munc13-1 and Munc13-2.
source: Thus, chromaffin cells can generate what appears to be a full-sized pool of morphologically docked LDCVs in the absence of Munc13-1 and Munc13-2, which implies that the molecular requirements of morphological LDCV and SV docking are distinct.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that LDCV docking is normal in Munc13-deficient cells.

claim: The molecular requirements of morphological LDCV and SV docking are distinct.
source: Thus, chromaffin cells can generate what appears to be a full-sized pool of morphologically docked LDCVs in the absence of Munc13-1 and Munc13-2, which implies that the molecular requirements of morphological LDCV and SV docking are distinct.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that LDCVs dock normally without Munc13s while SVs do not.

claim: The estimated size of the morphologically docked pool was approximately 662 LDCVs per chromaffin cell in control cells.
source: The estimated size of the morphologically docked pool was ∼662 LDCVs per chromaffin cell in control cells.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from EM data.

claim: For Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells, approximately 865 docked LDCVs per cell were calculated.
source: For Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells we calculated ∼865 docked LDCVs per cell, which can be accounted for by two factors used in the calculation: Unc13aKOUnc13bKO cells are slightly larger, and their LDCVs are slightly smaller (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from EM data.

claim: The size of the RRP corresponds to less than 44 vesicles from the total of approximately 662 docked vesicles in control cells.
source: Thereby, the size of the RRP, which is <40 fF at resting [Ca2+] (Voets, 2000), corresponds to <44 vesicles from the total of ∼662 in control cells, indicating that even with 3D-ET, the RRP will be very hard or even impossible to distinguish morphologically from other docked vesicles in adrenal chromaffin cells.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations combining EM and electrophysiology data.

claim: Even with 3D-ET, the RRP will be very hard or even impossible to distinguish morphologically from other docked vesicles in adrenal chromaffin cells.
source: Thereby, the size of the RRP, which is <40 fF at resting [Ca2+] (Voets, 2000), corresponds to <44 vesicles from the total of ∼662 in control cells, indicating that even with 3D-ET, the RRP will be very hard or even impossible to distinguish morphologically from other docked vesicles in adrenal chromaffin cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the calculation that the RRP represents a small fraction of docked vesicles.

claim: Munc13-1 and ubMunc13-2 promote LDCV priming with very similar steady-state Ca2+-affinities.
source: Strikingly, the Ca2+-dependence was almost identical for the two isoforms and could be fitted with a single Hill equation (Figure 7A right-hand panel, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and Hill equation fitting shown in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: Secretion driven solely by ubMunc13-2 shows a characteristic sigmoid shape at low pre-stimulus [Ca2+].
source: Secretion driven solely by the dominant isoform ubMunc13-2 shows a characteristic sigmoid shape at low pre-stimulus [Ca2+] (Figure 7C) (Zikich et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and citation to prior literature.

claim: The fitted maximum priming rate (k1) for ubMunc13-2 is 4.5-fold higher than for Munc13-1.
source: Thus, the fitted maximum priming rate (k1) for ubMunc13-2 is 4.5-fold higher than for Munc13-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Table 1.

claim: ubMunc13-2 shows 2.5-fold slower sensing of [Ca2+] than Munc13-1.
source: In the model, this delay is due to slower kinetics of Ca2+ binding to the priming sensor (Zikich et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Table 1.

claim: Munc13-1 reacts faster to a change in the [Ca2+] concentration than ubMunc13-2.
source: However, although Munc13-1 is unable to support the same maximum priming rate as ubMunc13-2, it reacts faster to a change in the [Ca2+] concentration (Figure 7B), which may reflect distinct conformational changes in response to [Ca2+], and/or differences in a membrane translocation step.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The action of Munc13 (either isoform) is consistent with an increase in k1, the forward rate of priming within the first priming step.
source: The modeling resulted in two main conclusions (Table 1): First, as expected, the action of Munc13 (either isoform) is consistent with an increase in k1 – the forward rate of priming within the first priming step (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Table 1 and Figure 7E.

claim: k2, the forward rate of downstream priming, always changed in the opposite direction of k1.
source: As a minor note, we also noticed that k2, the forward rate of downstream priming ('priming 2', Figure 7E) always changed in the opposite direction of k1.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The protein(s) driving downstream priming may compete with Munc13 for association with the fusion machinery.
source: The reason for this is unclear, but one explanation could be that the protein(s) driving downstream priming compete with Munc13 for association with the fusion machinery.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning to explain the observation that k2 changes opposite to k1.

claim: The essential role of Munc13s in vesicular release lies in the opening of Syntaxin (Stx-1)/Munc18-1 complexes.
source: The essential role of Munc13s in vesicular release appears to lie in the opening of Syntaxin (Stx-1)/Munc18-1 complexes, to permit the formation of Stx-1/SNAP-25 heterodimers that act as docking platforms for the vesicular SNARE protein Synaptobrevin-2 (Syb-2) (Hammarlund et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2013; Richmond et al., 1999; Sassa et al., 1999; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SNARE complex assembly is thought to proceed in an N- to C-terminal zipper-like fashion.
source: SNARE complex assembly is thought to proceed in an N- to C-terminal zipper-like fashion (Fasshauer and Margittai, 2004; Pobbati et al., 2006; Sorensen et al., 2006; Walter et al., 2010), and, at least for SVs, this assembly seems to be the molecular correlate of both the physical docking process, and acquisition of fusion competence, which is referred to as priming (Imig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For SVs, SNARE complex assembly seems to be the molecular correlate of both the physical docking process and acquisition of fusion competence (priming).
source: SNARE complex assembly is thought to proceed in an N- to C-terminal zipper-like fashion (Fasshauer and Margittai, 2004; Pobbati et al., 2006; Sorensen et al., 2006; Walter et al., 2010), and, at least for SVs, this assembly seems to be the molecular correlate of both the physical docking process, and acquisition of fusion competence, which is referred to as priming (Imig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Morphological docking of LDCVs does not require Munc13s, yet the priming of a full-sized RRP does.
source: However, as will be discussed below, morphological docking of LDCVs does not require Munc13s (Figure 6), yet the priming of a full-sized RRP does (Figure 2), indicating that LDCV docking and functional priming do not represent a one-step process in neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: LDCV docking and functional priming do not represent a one-step process in neuroendocrine cells.
source: However, as will be discussed below, morphological docking of LDCVs does not require Munc13s (Figure 6), yet the priming of a full-sized RRP does (Figure 2), indicating that LDCV docking and functional priming do not represent a one-step process in neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that docking and priming have different molecular requirements.

claim: In synapses, most, if not all docked SVs are part of the RRP.
source: Thus, in contrast to synapses, where most, if not all docked SVs are part of the RRP, the majority of docked LDCVs in chromaffin cells are not primed, and the functional RRP therefore cannot be distinguished from other docked LDCVs by current ultrastructural methods.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about synapses.

claim: The majority of docked LDCVs in chromaffin cells are not primed.
source: Thus, in contrast to synapses, where most, if not all docked SVs are part of the RRP, the majority of docked LDCVs in chromaffin cells are not primed, and the functional RRP therefore cannot be distinguished from other docked LDCVs by current ultrastructural methods.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the calculation that the RRP is much smaller than the pool of docked vesicles.

claim: The functional RRP cannot be distinguished from other docked LDCVs by current ultrastructural methods.
source: Thus, in contrast to synapses, where most, if not all docked SVs are part of the RRP, the majority of docked LDCVs in chromaffin cells are not primed, and the functional RRP therefore cannot be distinguished from other docked LDCVs by current ultrastructural methods.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the RRP is a small fraction of docked vesicles.

claim: Munc13-1 causes short term depression in autaptic neurons.
source: Previous data from autaptic neurons showed that Munc13-1 causes short term depression, whereas ubMunc13-2 causes short-term facilitation (Rosenmund et al., 2002), which parallels our findings in chromaffin cells from low basal [Ca2+], raising the possibility that the functions of different Munc13 isoforms in priming LDCVs and SVs are conserved, even though their role in docking is not.
